story: Rapamycin lengthens life in mice, but mice are far from people. Elizabeth Fernandez is a co-author of two Atlas studies that tried the drug in the common marmoset, a small, short-lived monkey. The 2014 study (TAR2014) worked out how to give rapamycin by mouth in a coated form, reached blood levels similar to those in mouse and human work, and saw lower mTORC1 signalling, the growth-control pathway, in the animals' tissues. The 2015 study (ROS2015) found that long-term treatment had only minor effects on body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling. Neither study measured lifespan.

Fernandez is also a co-author of a 2022 report from the NIA Interventions Testing Program (STR2022), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin combined with acarbose, a diabetes drug, gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had in earlier cohorts. In females the combination was no better than rapamycin alone.

PubMed places Fernandez at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and at the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the South Texas Veterans Health Care System on papers from 2014 to 2026. A 2026 paper with Randy Strong found that long-term rapamycin protected aging mice against the decline in motor function, with a larger effect in females. A current job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

current.lab_name: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Yinchuan, Ningxia, China)
current.role: Neurologist in Yinchuan who leads cell studies of microglia, the brain's immune cells, and of how Brucella bacteria survive inside them
current.sub: Neurology Center and Diagnosis and Treatment Engineering Technology Research Center of Nervous System Diseases of Ningxia, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (papers 2011–2026)
story: Brucellosis is an infection passed from farm animals to people, and it can reach the brain. The bacteria survive inside immune cells instead of being destroyed. Zhenhai Wang was senior author of LI2026B, a 2026 paper in the Journal of Medical Microbiology that asked how a Brucella strain does this in microglia, the immune cells of the brain. The team used BV2 cells, a mouse microglia cell line, infected with Brucella suis vaccine strain 2. The bacteria pushed the cells into a mixed state between M1 (the inflammatory, bacteria-killing mode) and M2 (the calmer, repair mode) and switched on autophagy. The M2 state and autophagy together helped the bacteria multiply inside the cells, and the effect ran through the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway.

Normally, autophagy helps immune cells destroy invading microbes. This study suggests that some bacteria can turn it to their own advantage, with mTOR signalling as part of the switch. It was done in a cell line, so it shows a possible mechanism and not what happens in infected patients.

Wang works in neurology at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University in Yinchuan and in the hospital's engineering research centre for nervous system diseases. The group's PubMed record goes back to a 2011 study of how hepatitis C virus stimulates mouse microglia, and includes a cerebrospinal fluid research laboratory, BV2 cell lines engineered to lack particular phosphatases, a 2024 study on how exosomes from microglia affect myelin repair, and a 2025 study on how doxycycline kills human microglial cells infected with the same Brucella strain.

studies.title: Brucella suis vaccine strain 2 promotes intracellular proliferation by inducing M2 macrophage polarization and autophagy through PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling.

current.role: Metabolism researcher who trained with Michael Hall in Basel on mTOR in fat tissue and now leads a group at KU Leuven studying how fat and liver control sugar and lipid storage
current.sub: Group leader, Clinical and Experimental Endocrinology, KU Leuven (last-author papers from 2023) · Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (to about 2023)
story: In 2014 Mitsugu Shimobayashi and Michael Hall wrote the review "Making new contacts" in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology. It describes mTOR as a hub in a network: the two mTOR complexes trade signals with other pathways, such as insulin and AMPK signalling, and between them steer how cells take up and use nutrients. A review collects earlier findings and does not add new experiments.

Shimobayashi also appears on two research papers in this Atlas. In a 2013 Science study, a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins showed that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on the cell's own production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. In 2020 a cryo-electron microscopy structure of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution pointed to the tail end of the subunit Rictor as the reason this complex is not blocked by rapamycin. These were cell and protein studies.

In Basel, Shimobayashi worked on mTOR in fat tissue and the whole body. A 2023 paper with Shimobayashi as senior author showed that when mTORC2 is lost in fat, mTORC2 in the liver can step in to keep energy storage and blood sugar in balance in mice. Shimobayashi now runs a group at KU Leuven in Belgium. Its 2025 papers show how a chemical tag on the protein MLX stabilises the sugar-sensing ChREBP-MLX complex on DNA to control carbohydrate and fat metabolism, and test a diet change after incretin-drug treatment in obese mice.

studies.title: Making new contacts: the mTOR network in metabolism and signalling crosstalk

story: Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can damage the brain, leaving survivors with memory problems. In the Atlas study YU2026, led by first author Jiafeng Yu with Yang Yu and Yonghao Yu as corresponding authors, septic mice had overactive mTOR in the medial prefrontal cortex. This kept oligodendrocyte precursor cells from maturing into the cells that make myelin, the insulation around nerve fibres, and the mice lost myelin and memory. Breathing high-concentration hydrogen gas lowered mTOR activity, restored myelin and improved memory; rapamycin had a similar effect. The work was done in mice.

Hydrogen gas is studied as a mild antioxidant and anti-inflammatory treatment. On PubMed, Yang Yu appears with Yonghao Yu in the Department of Anesthesiology at Tianjin Medical University General Hospital on earlier hydrogen studies in septic mice, including a 2020 paper showing that hydrogen protected the gut in severe sepsis through the Nrf2 pathway. Rank and training could not be confirmed.

studies.title: High-concentration hydrogen mitigates cognitive impairment in a murine model of Sepsis-associated encephalopathy by enhancing oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination in the mPFC

current.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Medical Faculty and University Hospital Düsseldorf, Heinrich Heine University (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
current.role: Cell biologist in Düsseldorf who studies the ULK1 complex, the switch that starts autophagy, and how it is wired to the energy sensor AMPK and to mTOR
current.sub: Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (papers 2015–2026) · Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (at the time of LOF2011)
story: Autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system, is started by a protein kinase called ULK1. When energy runs low, the energy sensor AMPK switches ULK1 on, and when nutrients are plentiful mTORC1 switches it off. In LOF2011, from Björn Stork's group, then at the University of Tübingen, Antje Löffler and colleagues found that the signal also runs backwards: ULK1 adds phosphate groups to AMPK and dampens its activity. This makes a negative feedback loop, a built-in way for the autophagy machinery to limit the signal that started it, rather than a one-way switch. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Stork's group later moved to the Institute of Molecular Medicine I at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, where it continued to dissect the ULK1 complex. In 2015 the team mapped the short stretch of the protein ATG13 that holds ULK1 in place and found that cells lacking this contact still keep some autophagy, which points to routes that bypass the usual ULK1-ATG13 link. In 2026, as senior author, Stork reported that human induced pluripotent stem cells and nerve progenitor cells have working autophagy machinery but do not switch it on after low-dose DNA damage, unlike many cancer cell lines.

studies.title: Ulk1-mediated phosphorylation of AMPK constitutes a negative regulatory feedback loop

current.role: Orthopedic researcher at Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and senior author of a 2026 mouse study showing that the plant compound corilagin slows osteoarthritis by restoring cartilage-cell autophagy
current.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: In osteoarthritis the cartilage that cushions joints slowly breaks down. Chondrocytes, the cells that maintain cartilage, depend on autophagy, their internal recycling system, and autophagy falls when PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling is too high. The 2026 study led by Ruijia Zhou, with Hongbo You as senior author, tested corilagin, a polyphenol found in several medicinal plants.

Corilagin lowered PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB signalling, the second being a main switch for inflammation. Chondrocytes recovered their autophagic flux and made more extracellular matrix, the material that gives cartilage its strength. In mice with surgically induced osteoarthritis (the DMM model, in which a knee ligament is cut to destabilise the joint), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and lowered OARSI damage scores. These are cell and mouse results; corilagin has not been tested in people with osteoarthritis.

PubMed lists Hongbo You at the Department of Orthopedics of Tongji Hospital in Wuhan, where You has co-authored papers with Fengjing Guo, senior author of the Atlas review on mTORC2 in inflammation. Career details could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: Corilagin attenuates osteoarthritis progression by coordinating NF-κB inhibition with PI3K/AKT/mTOR-associated autophagy restoration.

story: Johannes Beckers is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Beckers works at the Institute of Experimental Genetics of Helmholtz Munich in Neuherberg, near Munich, and PubMed records also list the Chair of Experimental Genetics at the Technical University of Munich and the German Center for Diabetes Research. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. In both Atlas papers Beckers appears among the German Mouse Clinic authors. Beckers's own papers centre on measuring which genes are switched on in tissues, for example with Marion Horsch and Martin Irmler, and range from mouse genetics to the effects of air pollution on the lung, as in a 2026 study of wood-smoke aerosols.

story: Rick K. Huang is a co-author on two Atlas studies from David Sabatini's laboratory, led by Kuang Shen, that used cryo-electron microscopy to see how amino acid signals reach mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cryo-EM freezes purified proteins in thin ice and builds a 3D model from many thousands of electron microscope images. The Rag GTPases are a pair of switch proteins on the lysosome surface that pull mTORC1 there when amino acids are present.

The 2018 Nature paper (SHE2018) showed the shape of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rags off when amino acids are scarce, alone and bound to the Rags. It revealed both the part that speeds up the Rags' GTP burning and a second, unexpected grip that holds them in place. The 2019 Cell paper (SHE2019) showed folliculin with its partner FNIP2 sitting on the Rags and on Ragulator, the platform that anchors them to the lysosome. Both studies used purified human proteins and biochemical tests, not cells or animals.
Both papers list Huang at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. A current position could not be confirmed with certainty.

story: Dean Quinn is a co-author of two Atlas papers on whether short, low-dose courses of mTOR-blocking drugs can make older people's immune systems work better. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of BEZ235 and everolimus was followed by fewer reported infections over the next year, more active antiviral genes and a better response to the flu vaccine. MAN2021 then tested BEZ235 alone (renamed RTB101) in two bigger trials. The phase 2b trial (652 people) showed fewer lab-confirmed respiratory infections only in an analysis that was not corrected for multiple testing, and the phase 3 trial (1,024 people) found no difference in its main endpoint. Taken together, these are human trials that gave an early signal and then a negative confirmatory result, a useful lesson in how drug evidence develops.

Trials like these recruit volunteers at specialised research clinics. PubMed lists Quinn at P3 Research in Newtown, Wellington, a clinical trials company in New Zealand, on about ten trial reports, and the 2021 paper also lists him with resTORbio, the Boston company that ran the RTB101 program.
No official profile was found to confirm Quinn's medical training or current position, so this profile is limited to what the publications show.

story: Kivanç Birsoy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute. The 2012 Nature paper (YIL2012) showed in mice that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, the cells that sit next to intestinal stem cells and support them. With less mTORC1, Paneth cells send signals that make the neighbouring stem cells more numerous and more active. The 2014 Cancer Discovery paper (GRA2014) went through MTOR mutations found in human cancers, identified 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse tumour grafts. That suggests the mutations could help pick patients who might respond to mTOR inhibitors.

Birsoy's own first-author work in the Sabatini laboratory was on cell metabolism. A 2015 Cell paper used a CRISPR screen to find genes that cells need when their mitochondria are blocked by the drug phenformin. It showed that one essential job of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in dividing cells is to let them make the amino acid aspartate, and that cells without a working chain can grow if they get extra aspartate.

Birsoy now leads the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at The Rockefeller University in New York. The lab continues to combine genetic screens with metabolism; a 2026 paper in Cell Chemical Biology, for example, used CRISPR screens to identify TXNDC15 as a missing part of the system that removes faulty proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, with effects on lipid balance.

story: Yoshinori Ito is a co-author of the two BOLERO-2 papers in the Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had grown despite an aromatase inhibitor. In such tumours, resistance to hormone therapy is linked to overactive mTOR signalling. All women received the hormone drug exemestane, and half also received everolimus, an mTORC1 inhibitor related to rapamycin.

BAS2012, in the New England Journal of Medicine, reported the main result: adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, from 4.1 to 10.6 months by central review, which led to approval of the combination. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis). PIC2014, in Annals of Oncology, gave the final overall survival: 31.0 months with everolimus and 26.6 months with placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant. Together the two papers show both what mTOR blockade can do in a common cancer and its limits.

In large international trials like this, many hospitals enrol patients, and their investigators appear as co-authors. PubMed lists about fifty breast cancer papers under this name from the Department of Breast Medical Oncology of the Cancer Institute Hospital. No official profile was opened, so the current title is not given here.

current.role: Graduate researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and first author of a 2017 study reporting that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids restores metabolic health

story: Nicole Cummings is a co-author of two linked mouse studies from Dudley Lamming's lab in this Atlas (ARR2015, ARR2016). Rapamycin is the best-tested drug for extending lifespan in mice, but given every day it causes side effects such as poor blood sugar control and weaker immune responses. In ARR2015, mice given rapamycin daily (2 mg/kg) became glucose intolerant and their insulin-producing islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every five days left glucose and insulin tolerance normal, while dosing every three days was already too frequent. In ARR2016, female mice that started the every-five-days schedule at 20 months of age, which is old for a mouse, lived longer than untreated females. Taken together, the two mouse studies suggest that rapamycin's lifespan benefit can be partly separated from its side effects by giving it intermittently. This conclusion comes from combining two experiments in mice, not from a single study, and has not been tested this way in people.

Cummings trained in the University of Wisconsin-Madison's graduate program in endocrinology and reproductive physiology while working in Lamming's lab. The main line of that work was diet: branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine and valine) are building blocks of protein, and leucine is a strong activator of mTORC1. Cummings was second author of a 2016 Cell Reports paper showing that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids improves metabolic health, and first author of a 2017 Journal of Physiology paper reporting that the same diet change can restore metabolic health. Cummings also wrote a 2016 review, as first author, on how nutrient-sensing signalling pathways regulate metabolic health and aging, and co-authored studies on methionine restriction (2018) and on how calorie restriction improves insulin sensitivity through mTORC2 in fat tissue (2019).
No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

current.lab_name: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Department of Oncology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
current.role: Immunologist trained in Jonathan Powell's lab at Johns Hopkins who used gene deletions in mice to show how the two mTOR complexes push killer T cells toward effector or memory fates
current.sub: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, 2011–2016; latest PubMed affiliation)
story: CD8 T cells are the immune system's killer cells. After an infection, most become short-lived effectors that attack, and a few become long-lived memory cells that guard against the next infection. Kristen Pollizzi's 2015 study in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, with Jonathan Powell as senior author, used mice whose T cells lacked Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor to separate the roles of the two mTOR complexes. With Tsc2 gone, mTORC1 stayed switched on: the cells burned glucose hard, made more of the killing molecules IFN-gamma, TNF and granzyme B, and controlled tumours better, but they ended up terminally differentiated, fewer in number after a month, and formed no memory. With Rheb gone, mTORC1 was off while mTORC2 still worked: these cells failed as effectors and kept memory-like features, yet they did not respond when the mice met the same antigen again, which the authors traced to defects in their metabolism.

The message is that mTOR activity tunes the balance between attack and memory, and that a T cell needs the right amount of each complex at the right time. That matters for vaccine design and for cancer treatments that rely on T cells. Pollizzi was also a co-author on the 2011 Nature Immunology paper from the same lab showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages.

PubMed lists 11 papers for Pollizzi between 2011 and 2016, all with the Powell group at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins. They include a 2015 PLoS One study showing that cell size after activation can be used to track mTOR activity and predict whether a T cell becomes an effector or a long-lived cell, and reviews on mTOR and T cell metabolism in Nature Reviews Immunology (2014) and Trends in Immunology (2015). No later publications or current position could be found.

story: Many drugs extend lifespan in one lab animal and then fail in the next. Kevin Perez is first author of a 2026 paper describing a platform built to tackle that problem (PEREZ2026). It tests compounds in yeast, nematode worms, fruit flies, killifish and mice, uses automated imaging and a deep-learning program to spot when each animal dies, and has screened more than 400 compounds under thousands of conditions. By comparing species, it picks out compounds that work in several of them and shows that hits tend to act on known conserved longevity pathways, mTOR among them. The paper is about methods and infrastructure; individual hits still need checking in mammals and eventually people.

PubMed lists Perez with both EPITERNA SA and Alejandro Ocampo's group in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Lausanne. Earlier work includes a 2023 first-author study showing that mouse models of premature aging with defects in DNA repair have an older 'epigenetic age', measured from DNA methylation, than their real age, unlike other premature aging models, and a 2025 study in which a two-chemical reprogramming cocktail reduced signs of aging in human cells and extended lifespan in worms.

story: Diogo Martins-Branco is first author of EVERGREEN (MAR2026), a study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite hormone therapy combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, today's standard first treatment. The question was whether adding everolimus, an mTOR blocker, to the next hormone therapy still helps. Across several centres, patients given everolimus went a little longer before the cancer grew again (median 5.0 versus 4.3 months) but did not clearly live longer.

Everolimus was approved for this kind of breast cancer before CDK4/6 inhibitors existed, so doctors need to know whether it still works after them. EVERGREEN gives a cautious answer: a small benefit, best kept for selected patients. The study looked back at patient records and was not randomised, so differences in who received the drug may have shaped the result.

Martins-Branco trained and worked as a medical oncologist in Lisbon, publishing from the breast clinic of the Instituto Português de Oncologia de Lisboa on topics such as using genomic tests to spare women chemotherapy. From about 2022 the papers list the Academic Trials Promoting Team at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels, which designs and runs large academic breast cancer trials, and work there included reviews on antibody-drug conjugates. A 2026 paper on the ESMO scale for ranking cancer gene targets lists the Scientific and Medical Division of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Lugano, Switzerland, which appears to be the current post.

current.lab_name: Rainero Lab, School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield (Sheffield, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: Cell biologist in Elena Rainero's lab at the University of Sheffield who studies how the collagen-rich matrix around tumours feeds cancer cells when nutrients run short
current.sub: School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield, Elena Rainero lab (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2020 to 2026)
story: Mona Nazemi is the first author of NAZ2026. Breast and pancreatic tumours are packed in collagen I, the main protein of scar-like tissue, and the blood supply in them is poor, so cancer cells are often short of amino acids. The study found that cancer cells sitting on collagen I use their collagen receptor, alpha2beta1 integrin, to switch on mTORC1 and its target S6, and to bring the amino acid transporter LAT1-4F2hc to the cell surface. More transporter at the surface means more essential amino acids get in, and the cells survive. In patient data, high LAT1-4F2hc levels in basal-like breast and pancreatic tumours went with a worse outlook. This links the tumour's surroundings directly to mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor.

Nazemi has worked with Elena Rainero at Sheffield since at least 2020, when they wrote a review on how the tumour matrix and cell metabolism talk to each other. In a 2024 PLoS Biology paper, also as first author, Nazemi showed that invasive breast cancer cells starved of amino acids can swallow pieces of the surrounding matrix, break them down in lysosomes and use the released tyrosine and phenylalanine to keep growing.
No official profile was found, so training and current role are given only from the publication record.

studies.title: Collagen I promotes cancer cell survival via amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activation

current.lab_name: Chakraverty Lab, UCL Cancer Institute, University College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: Haematologist and T-cell researcher at University College London who studies how engineered T cells behave in cancer therapy, and who showed that forcing mTORC1 on in CD4+ T cells makes them last longer but tire out
current.sub: Haematologist, University College London Hospitals and Royal Marsden Hospital (2025–2026) · Cancer Institute, University College London, with Ronjon Chakraverty and Hans Stauss (2019–2026) · Department of Haematology, Basildon University Hospital (2011)
story: Cancer treatments with engineered T cells, such as CAR-T and TCR-T cells, work only if the infused cells survive and keep fighting. In a 2026 Journal of Immunology paper, with Ronjon Chakraverty as senior author, Francesca Sillito made mouse CD4+ helper T cells produce extra RHEB, a protein that switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. After transfer into mice the cells first grew more and lasted longer, but over time they became exhausted: they carried brake-like receptors on their surface and divided poorly when they met their target again. CD8+ killer T cells had been reported to react differently to the same change. The study is in mice and warns that boosting mTORC1 in therapeutic T cells has a cost.

Sillito is a haematologist, a doctor who treats blood diseases and blood cancers. An early case report from 2011 lists Sillito at Basildon University Hospital. Sillito's research at University College London's Institute of Immunity and Transplantation and Cancer Institute focused on T-cell engineering; with Angelika Holler and Hans Stauss, Sillito wrote a 2020 review on engineering CD4+ T cells to strengthen cancer immunity.

Sillito's recent papers come from the clinic. As first author in Haematologica (2025), Sillito studied how blood stem-cell clones change after CAR-T therapy and the risk of later myeloid cancers, and has co-authored UK studies of second-line CAR-T treatment for large B-cell lymphoma from University College London Hospitals and the Royal Marsden Hospital.

studies.title: Enforcing mTORC1 activity in therapeutic CD4+ T cells promotes persistence but eventual immune exhaustion

current.lab_name: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea)
current.role: Medicinal chemist in Hyeon Soo Kim's group at the Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, who designs small molecules, and first author of the study of the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH that switches on mTORC1 through Sestrin2
current.sub: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Hyeon Soo Kim group, papers 2021–2026)
story: Muscle builds protein when mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on, and the amino acid leucine is one of its main triggers. Leucine works by binding a sensor protein called Sestrin2, which then lets go of the brake on mTORC1. In the Atlas study SHIM2026, Shim and colleagues made DLMEH, a modified form of D-leucine (the mirror-image form of normal leucine) designed as a prodrug, a compound the body converts into the active form. DLMEH bound Sestrin2 about as tightly as ordinary leucine and switched on mTORC1 only when Sestrin2 was present.

In human muscle cells grown in a dish, DLMEH restored protein production. In rats whose muscles were wasted by the steroid dexamethasone, it preserved muscle mass, grip strength and endurance. The rat model mimics steroid-induced muscle loss, not age-related sarcopenia, and no human trial has been done.

On PubMed, Shim's papers come from the Department of Anatomy at Korea University College of Medicine with Hyeon Soo Kim and are mostly chemistry: a 2021 paper on a catalyst that builds molecules with a chosen handedness, and a 2026 paper on a new oral pain-relief compound that blocks the Nav1.7 sodium channel in nerve cells. Rank could not be confirmed.

studies.title: D-Amino Acid Prodrug DLMEH Activates mTORC1 via Sestrin2 to Restore Muscle Protein Synthesis in Sarcopenia.

current.role: Cardiologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, working in interventional cardiology, and first author of a trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
current.sub: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine (Division of Interventional Cardiology), Mayo Clinic, Rochester (2023–2026) · Department of Internal Medicine, Mayo Clinic (2020–2021)
story: Conor Lane is first author of the Atlas entry LAN2026, a 2026 Mayo Clinic Proceedings report on rapamycin in frail older people who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In HFpEF the heart pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat but is stiff and fills poorly. It is common in older adults, and there are few treatments that help. Rapamycin, the classic mTOR blocker, slows aging processes in animals, so a trial in this group tests whether that idea carries over to a real age-related disease in people.

The team joined Mayo Clinic cardiologists, including senior author Mandeep Singh, with aging researchers James Kirkland at Mayo and Dudley Lamming and Judith Simcox at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The abstract was not yet public when the Atlas entry was made, so the results are not summarised here.

Lane's other papers trace a clinical career at Mayo Clinic in Rochester. In 2020 and 2021 PubMed lists the Department of Internal Medicine, on studies of heart ultrasound methods and of medicines linked to microscopic colitis. From 2023 the affiliation is cardiovascular medicine, with case reports and commentary on catheter-based treatments, such as removing infected material from a mitral valve, repairing a coronary aneurysm and opening a blocked bypass graft. By 2025 Lane is listed in the Division of Interventional Cardiology.

studies.title: Rapamycin in Frail Older Subjects with Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

current.lab_name: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences (Warsaw, Poland)
current.role: Leukemia researcher in Warsaw who works on new drug combinations for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including mTORC1 inhibitors that make leukemia cells easier targets for anti-CD20 antibodies
current.sub: Laboratory of Immunology, Mossakowski Medical Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences · Department of Immunology, Medical University of Warsaw (papers with Malgorzata Firczuk, 2024–2026)
story: B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is the most common childhood cancer. Antibody drugs such as rituximab attack cells that carry the surface protein CD20, but many BCP-ALL cells show little CD20, so the antibodies have few places to grab. In DAB2026, Agnieszka Dąbkowska and colleagues in Malgorzata Firczuk's group found that drugs blocking mTORC1, the growth-control complex, raise CD20 on these leukemia cells. The route runs through AKT and the transcription factor FOXO1, and the treated cells also move a step further along B-cell maturation. As a result, anti-CD20 antibodies killed leukemia cells better, including in high-risk disease with deletions in the IKZF1 gene. The study gives a laboratory rationale for combining mTORC1 inhibitors with CD20-targeted antibodies; it is not a clinical trial.

Dąbkowska works with the Firczuk group at the Mossakowski Medical Research Institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences and the Department of Immunology of the Medical University of Warsaw. In 2024 Dąbkowska was a co-author of a study showing that blocking the antioxidant enzyme peroxiredoxin-1 together with a DNA repair pathway makes Philadelphia-positive B-ALL much more sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: mTORC1 inhibition upregulates CD20 and enhances anti-CD20 antibody efficacy in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia

current.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
current.role: Neurology researcher in Suzhou and first author of a 2026 study on how the enzyme PIP4K2A protects the brain after stroke by restoring autophagy through AKT/mTOR
current.sub: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Restoring blood flow after a stroke saves brain tissue, but the sudden return of oxygen also injures cells. Bodun Ma's 2026 study, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, asked whether the lipid kinase PIP4K2A could limit this reperfusion damage.

In the team's experimental models, more PIP4K2A meant less injury. Two changes went with it: less of a TRIB3-p62 complex that can jam autophagy, the cell's recycling pathway, and altered AKT/mTOR signalling, which let autophagy flow again. mTOR normally holds autophagy back when growth signals are high, so tuning this pathway changes how well damaged neurons clear debris. These are laboratory findings, not results in stroke patients.
PubMed gives the Department of Neurology at the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University as Bodun Ma's affiliation. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: PIP4K2A Attenuates Cerebral Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury by Reducing the TRIB3-p62 Complex Burden and Modulating AKT/mTOR Signaling.

current.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
current.role: Orthopedic researcher at Union Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 study that found a new route by which failing autophagy switches on mTORC1 and drives spinal disc degeneration
current.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: The discs between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers, and their slow degeneration is a major cause of back pain. Xianglong Chen's 2026 study in Advanced Science, with Y. Zhang as senior author, focused on chaperone-mediated autophagy, a selective clean-up route in which single proteins are fed one by one into the lysosome through a receptor called LAMP2A.

In disc cells from patients and in rat models, this pathway was weakened. One of its usual cargoes, the protein midnolin, then built up. Midnolin bound TSC2, part of the main brake on mTORC1, and sent it to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, without the usual ubiquitin tag. With the brake gone, mTORC1 became overactive, and the disc cells became senescent, released inflammatory signals and lost their matrix. Reducing midnolin, adding back LAMP2A or giving rapamycin each blocked the damage in cells and rats. The study describes a new upstream route to mTORC1 overactivity; it has not been tested as a treatment in people.

PubMed lists Xianglong Chen at the Department of Orthopedics of Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

studies.title: Impaired Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy Accelerates Intervertebral Disc Degeneration by Inducing MIDN Accumulation to Target TSC2 for Proteasomal Degradation

current.lab_name: Yang Lab, Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Lexington, Kentucky, USA)
current.role: Cancer biologist in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab at the University of Kentucky who studies how the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 holds back mTORC2 signalling, protein synthesis and cancer cell invasion
current.sub: Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology and Markey Cancer Center, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky (Hsin-Sheng Yang lab, papers 2017–2026)
story: Cancer cells burn sugar fast, even when oxygen is plentiful, a habit called aerobic glycolysis. In the Atlas study WANG2026B in Neoplasia, Qing Wang was first author in Hsin-Sheng Yang's lab. The team showed in non-small cell lung cancer cells and in tumours grown in mice that the tumour suppressor Pdcd4 binds Rictor, the core partner of mTOR in the mTORC2 complex, through three positively charged amino acids (R105, K108 and R110). This binding breaks up mTORC2 and lowers its activity. Less mTORC2 means less PFKFB3, an enzyme that speeds up glycolysis, so the cancer cells use less sugar and grow more slowly. The work was done in cells and mouse xenografts.

Wang has worked with Yang in the Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology at the University of Kentucky for several years; PubMed lists 18 papers with both names and this address. Much of the work is on Pdcd4 in colorectal cancer. A 2025 first-author paper showed that Pdcd4 blocks translation of Slug, a protein that helps cancer cells invade, through the 5' untranslated region of its messenger RNA. A 2020 first-author paper found that blocking the IGF-1 receptor in colon cancer cells switches on MEK, a survival signal, which may explain why IGF-1 receptor drugs worked poorly in patients. No official profile page was found.

studies.title: Pdcd4-Rictor interaction suppresses mTORC2-PFKFB3 axis and tumorigenesis in NSCLC.

current.lab_name: De Virgilio Lab, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
current.role: Cell biologist at the University of Fribourg who studies TORC1 signalling in yeast and mammals, and first author of the discovery that malonyl-CoA is a natural mTORC1 inhibitor
current.sub: Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (papers 2016–2026, many with Claudio De Virgilio) · earlier papers with an affiliation in Milan, Italy (2014–2015)
story: Raffaele Nicastro is the first author of NIC2023, a Nature Cell Biology paper by groups at the University of Fribourg and Constantinos Demetriades's lab. mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that uses ATP to tag other proteins. The study found that malonyl-CoA, a small molecule made on the way to building fatty acids, fits directly into the mTOR catalytic pocket and competes with ATP. It works like a natural version of the ATP-competitive mTOR drugs. When the fat-making enzyme fatty acid synthase is turned down, malonyl-CoA builds up and dampens mTORC1. This ties the cell's capacity to make fat to its overall growth output. The effect was seen in yeast and mammalian cells, which is why the paper calls it conserved.

Nicastro's PubMed record shows many papers from the University of Fribourg between 2016 and 2026 many of them with Claudio De Virgilio, whose group studies how TORC1 is controlled in yeast. Papers from 2014 and 2015 list an affiliation in Milan, Italy. No official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Malonyl-CoA is a conserved endogenous ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor
